plain_english: Everyone's problems come from worrying about external things. Their helplessness comes from external things. "What should I do? How will this go? How will it turn out? Will this happen? Will that happen?" These are the words of people who focus on things outside their control. But who says "How can I avoid believing lies? How can I not turn away from truth?" If someone actually worries about these things, I'll remind them: Why are you anxious? This is in your power. Be confident. Don't rush to agree with something before you apply your natural ability to reason.
original_excerpt: The difficulties of all men are about external things, their helplessness is about external. What shall I do? how will it be? how will it turn out? will this happen? will that? All these are the words of those who are turning themselves to things which are not within the power of the will. For who says, How shall I not assent to that which is false? how shall I not turn away from the truth? If a man be of such a good disposition as to be anxious about these things I will remind him of this: Why are you anxious? The thing is in your own power, be assured; do not be precipitate in assenting before you apply the natural rule.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value, Section 1

plain_english: Now, if someone worries about their desires — whether they'll get what they want and avoid what they don't want — I'd actually respect them first. At least they're not wasting energy on the same trivial stuff everyone else obsesses over. They're focused on their own business and their own situation. But then I'd tell them: If you don't want to fail at getting what you desire, and you don't want to end up with what you're trying to avoid, then here's the solution. Don't desire anything that belongs to other people. Don't try to avoid anything that's outside your control. If you ignore this rule, you'll definitely fail to get what you want and end up with exactly what you're trying to avoid. What's so hard about this? Where's the confusion? Why ask 'How will this turn out?' or 'Will this happen or that?'
original_excerpt: On the other side, if a man is anxious (uneasy) about desire, lest it fail in its purpose and miss its end, and with respect to the avoidance of things, lest he should fall into that which he would avoid, I will first kiss (love) him, because he throws away the things about which others are in a flutter (others desire) and their fears, and employs his thoughts about his own affairs and his own condition. Then I shall say to him: If you do not choose to desire that which you will fail to obtain nor to attempt to avoid that into which you will fall, desire nothing which belongs to (which is in the power of) others, nor try to avoid any of the things which are not in your power. If you do not observe this rule, you must of necessity fail in your desires and fall into that which you would avoid. What is the difficulty here? where is there room for the words How will it be? and How will it turn out? and Will this happen or that?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value, Section 1

plain_english: Now, isn't what happens outside your will's control? Yes. And good and evil — don't they exist in things your will does control? Yes. So can you handle whatever happens according to nature? Can anyone stop you? No one can. So stop asking me, "How will things turn out?" However they turn out, you'll handle them well. The result will be good for you. What would Hercules have been if he'd said, "What if a giant lion shows up? Or a massive boar? Or violent men?" Who cares about that? If a giant boar appears, you'll fight an even greater fight. If bad men appear, you'll rid the earth of them. But what if I die doing this? Then you'll die as a good person, doing something noble. Since you must die anyway, death will find you doing something — farming, digging, trading, serving as a consul, or suffering from stomach problems or diarrhea. So what do you want to be doing when death finds you?
original_excerpt: Now is not that which will happen independent of the will? Yes. And the nature of good and of evil, is it not in the things which are within the power of the will? Yes. Is it in your power then to treat according to nature everything which happens? Can any person hinder you? No man. No longer then say to me, How will it be? For, however it may be, you will dispose of it well, and the result to you will be a fortunate one. What would Hercules have been if he said: How shall a great lion not appear to me, or a great boar, or savage men? And what do you care for that? If a great boar appear, you will fight a greater fight; if bad men appear, you will relieve the earth of the bad. Suppose then that I lose my life in this way. You will die a good man, doing a noble act. For since he must certainly die, of necessity a man must be found doing something, either following the employment of a husbandman, or digging, or trading, or serving in a consulship, or suffering from indigestion or from diarrhoea. What then do you wish to be doing when you are found by death?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value, Section 1

plain_english:
I want to be found doing something worthy of a human being — something helpful, good for everyone, and noble. But if I can't manage anything that great, I'd at least want to be found doing what no one can stop me from doing. What I'm always allowed to do: improving myself, training my mind to handle impressions properly, working toward freedom from destructive emotions, and working toward peace of mind. I want to give each relationship in my life what it deserves. If I succeed at that, I'd also want to make progress on the third area: being safe and sound in my judgments about things.

If death catches me busy with these things, that's enough for me. I could stretch out my hands to God and say: 'The tools you gave me to understand how you run the world and to follow along — I didn't neglect them. I didn't dishonor you with my actions. Look how I used my perceptions. Look how I used my basic concepts. Did I ever blame you? Was I ever unhappy with what happened, or wish things were different? Did I ever want to break the natural order of things? You gave me life, and I thank you for what you gave me. As long as I used your gifts properly, I'm content. Take them back and put them wherever you want — everything was yours to begin with. You just lent them to me.'

Isn't that enough — to die with this attitude? What life is better and more fitting than the life of someone in this frame of mind? What death is happier?
original_excerpt: I, for my part, would wish to be found doing something which belongs to a man, beneficent, suitable to the general interest, noble. But if I cannot be found doing things so great, I would be found doing at least that which I cannot be hindered from doing, that which is permitted me to do, correcting myself, cultivating the faculty which makes use of appearances, laboring at freedom from the affects (laboring at tranquillity of mind); rendering to the relations of life their due. If I succeed so far, also (I would be found) touching on (advancing to) the third topic (or head) safety in forming judgments about things. If death surprises me when I am busy about these things, it is enough for me if I can stretch out my hands to God and say: The means which I have received from thee for seeing thy administration (of the world) and following it I have not neglected; I have not dishonored thee by my acts; see how I have used my perceptions, see how I have used my preconceptions; have I ever blamed thee? have I been discontented with anything that happens, or wished it to be otherwise? have I wished to transgress the (established) relations (of things)? That thou hast given me life, I thank thee for what thou hast given. So long as I have used the things which are thine I am content. Take them back and place them wherever thou mayest choose, for thine were all things, thou gavest them to me. Is it not enough to depart in this state of mind? and what life is better and more becoming than that of a man who is in this state of mind? and what end is more happy?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value, Section 1
